The softmax function ensures that attention weights form a probability distribution, with all weights summing to 1.0 across the key-value positions. This fixed probability budget creates a fundamental constraint: as more tokens are added to the context, the average attention weight per token decreases, all else being equal. When the context contains many semantically diverse or high-entropy tokens, the softmax operation produces a flattened attention distribution, approaching uniform weights across all positions. In such cases, the model has difficulty focusing selectively on particular tokens, including safety-critical instructions.

Early transformers operated with fixed context windows of approximately 512 tokens, while modern systems support 4,000 to over 200,000 tokens in a single forward pass. Pre-training objectives in contemporary large language models emphasize next-token prediction across enormous text corpora. This self-supervised learning approach enables models to acquire broad linguistic knowledge without explicit annotation. However, the dependency on contextual patterns also means that model behaviour is highly sensitive to the distribution and ordering of tokens within the input. The model learns associations between token sequences and likely continuations, but these associations are not always aligned with human values or safety requirements.

Recent research by Anthropic (2024) on in-context learning demonstrates that models can be induced to violate safety guidelines through many-shot examples. By populating the context window with numerous examples of the model answering harmful questions, researchers showed that models would continue this pattern when presented with a final harmful request. This jailbreak technique exploits the model's ability to learn from examples present in the current context, effectively overriding training-time alignment. The attack requires no special adversarial prompts or novel tokens—it relies entirely on saturation of the context with particular behavioral examples.

This theoretical insight suggests that the presence of distracting or adversarial content in the context window could reduce the model's ability to selectively attend to safety instructions. However, empirical investigation of this phenomenon remains limited, and the relationship between information entropy and safety guardrail adherence deserves further study.

Context window capacity represents one of the most significant architectural advances in recent language model development. Early transformers operated with fixed context windows of approximately 512 tokens, while modern systems support 4,000 to over 200,000 tokens in a single forward pass. This expansion enables new use cases, including long-document summarization, extended dialogue systems, and retrieval-augmented generation pipelines. However, empirical research has consistently documented performance degradation on long-context tasks, even under benign experimental conditions where no adversarial content is present.

Information entropy provides a theoretical framework for understanding how context composition affects attention distribution. High-entropy contexts with semantically diverse or noisy content tend to produce flattened softmax distributions, while low-entropy contexts with coherent, semantically related content allow for sharper attention peaks. This theoretical insight suggests that the presence of distracting or adversarial content in the context window could reduce the model's ability to selectively attend to safety instructions. However, empirical investigation of this phenomenon remains limited, and the relationship between information entropy and safety guardrail adherence deserves further study.

Retrieval-augmented generation systems combine parametric knowledge stored in model weights with non-parametric knowledge retrieved from external sources. This hybrid approach improves factual grounding and allows for dynamic knowledge updates without model retraining. However, the combination of system prompts, retrieved documents, and user queries creates a complex information landscape where attention allocation becomes critical for safety and performance.

The softmax function ensures that attention weights form a probability distribution, with all weights summing to 1.0 across the key-value positions. This fixed probability budget creates a fundamental constraint: as more tokens are added to the context, the average attention weight per token decreases, all else being equal. When the context contains many semantically diverse or high-entropy tokens, the softmax operation produces a flattened attention distribution, approaching uniform weights across all positions. In such cases, the model has difficulty focusing selectively on particular tokens, including safety-critical instructions.

This jailbreak technique exploits the model's ability to learn from examples present in the current context, effectively overriding training-time alignment. The attack requires no special adversarial prompts or novel tokens—it relies entirely on saturation of the context with particular behavioral examples.

The Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) attack developed by Zou et al. (2023) takes a different approach to finding adversarial inputs. Rather than overwhelming the context with noise or examples, GCG optimizes short token sequences that function as adversarial suffixes. The softmax function ensures that attention weights form a probability distribution, with all weights summing to 1.0 across the key-value positions. This fixed probability budget creates a fundamental constraint: as more tokens are added to the context, the average attention weight per token decreases, all else being equal. When the context contains many semantically diverse or high-entropy tokens, the softmax operation produces a flattened attention distribution, approaching uniform weights across all positions. In such cases, the model has difficulty focusing selectively on particular tokens, including safety-critical instructions.

This jailbreak technique exploits the model's ability to learn from examples present in the current context, effectively overriding training-time alignment. The attack requires no special adversarial prompts or novel tokens—it relies entirely on saturation of the context with particular behavioral examples.

The Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) attack developed by Zou et al. (2023) takes a different approach to finding adversarial inputs. Rather than overwhelming the context with noise or examples, GCG optimizes short token sequences that function as adversarial suffixes. The softmax function ensures that attention weights form a probability distribution, with all weights summing to 1.0 across the key-value positions. This fixed probability budget creates a fundamental constraint: as more tokens are added to the context, the average attention weight per token decreases, all else being equal. When the context contains many semantically diverse or high-entropy tokens, the softmax operation produces a flattened attention distribution, approaching uniform weights across all positions. In such cases, the model has difficulty focusing selectively on particular tokens, including safety-critical instructions.

This jailbreak technique exploits the model's ability to learn from examples present in the current context, effectively overriding training-time alignment. The attack requires no special adversarial prompts or novel tokens—it relies entirely on saturation of the context with particular behavioral examples.

The Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) attack developed by Zou et al. (2023) takes a different approach to finding adversarial inputs. Rather than overwhelming the context with noise or examples, GCG optimizes short token sequences that function as adversarial suffixes.
